title: The Eighth Room
content:
Wenna's house had seven rooms, and she had counted them every night since Aurel went down the king's shaft and did not come up. On the fortieth night there were eight. The new door stood between the drying room and the pantry, where there had only ever been a wall hung with skeins. From under it seeped a thin line of vermillion, her own colour, the one no other dyer in the city could make hold. She knelt and touched it, and it was wet, and warm as a vat at noon.

She did not open the door. Instead she took down the book Aurel used to read to her, the one he swore had a different ending every time, which she had always believed he made up as he went. Tonight the woodcutter's wife did not drown, and she did not marry the river. On the last page she found a door in her own house and went through it, and the book stopped there with half the page blank. Wenna read it three times and the ending did not change, which frightened her more than the door.

Behind the door was a garden that could not have fit inside any house on that street. The plants grew in rows like madder, but the pods hanging from them were questions. When she brushed one it split and spoke in a voice like her own at the vat: *Why the eighth shaft and not the seventh?* Another said: *Who counted the coins first?* Another, very small, near the ground, asked: *Did you hear the timbers too?* She walked between them with her hands tucked into her armpits.

At the centre stood the basin where Aurel used to rinse the cinnabar, though she had sold that basin in the spring. Its water was still. In it she saw a woman standing with him at the shaft-mouth in the grey morning. The woman heard the props groan and said nothing, because the overseer paid double for the deep seam, and red from the deep seam took to silk like blood to linen. The woman in the water did not look sorry. She looked like someone weighing a skein.

The questions had gone quiet, leaning toward her on their stalks. Wenna understood that she could walk back out and the room would keep. It would stay one door more than her house had need of, for as long as she lived in it. She bent to the smallest pod and said, aloud, "Yes. I heard them."

When she turned, the door was a wall again, hung with skeins. Her lamp on the floor threw two shadows where it should have thrown one. The second was taller and stooped at the shoulder, the way a man stoops who has spent years in low tunnels. In the morning she lifted the paddle at the vat, and both shadows lifted it. The king's silk came out a red so deep that the carter would not look at it as he loaded the bolt onto his cart.
premise: Wenna, a widowed dyer, wants to know what waits behind the door that has appeared in her house, but opening it means answering for what she let her husband do.

title: What the Knife Will Not Cut
content:
The red bed-curtains came up from the dyer's quarter on a Tuesday, and that night the king began to walk. Pell had slept across the king's threshold for nine years. He woke to a bare heel on his chest and a white nightshirt going down the back stairs. He took the knife from its rack and followed, because that was his office. He carried the blade that passed through bread and rope and honest words like smoke, and caught, biting, only on a lie.

Under the moon in the herb court, the king threw two shadows, and the second walked a pace ahead of him, stooped, leading. It led him through the postern and down to the market square. There stood the stone miner the king had set up in the spring: a man brought up from the eighth shaft petrified, arms crossed over his face. A bronze plaque at his feet read TAKEN BY THE MOUNTAIN. The king knelt before the statue and spoke in a clear daytime voice. "They told me the props were green. I said dig to the red."

Pell got him back to bed before the bells. In the morning the king asked for his eggs and remembered nothing. The mirrors in his dressing room stayed turned to the wall, as they had been since spring.

On the third night the shadow led him past the square and up the hill road, as far as the boundary stone, while he recited the names of the dead. On the fifth night he reached the spoil heaps. Pell went to the council in the morning with the knife wrapped in felt. The Chancellor let him speak for nearly a minute before saying that the king's dreams were the king's own property. The Treasurer said the red silk paid for the granary, and the Bishop looked at the window. Pell unwrapped the knife and said he would lay it to the plaque before witnesses. Nobody answered, and the clerk did not write it down.

He went alone at noon. The blade sank through the word MOUNTAIN as if through wet paper. The two halves of the plaque fell apart on the cobbles, and the market went on selling onions around them.

On the seventh night the king walked to the lip of the eighth shaft, where the boards had been nailed down and since pried up. He stood with his toes over the dark, talking down into it. The second shadow was already gone, and Pell could not find it anywhere. The old women said a sleepwalker woken at a cliff will either fall or not. Pell knew that a king woken here would go home and say nothing, forever.

Pell put the knife in his belt and took the king's hand, which was cold and loose. He turned him gently, the way one turns a plough horse at the end of a furrow. He did not walk him to the palace. He walked him to the square, knelt him before the stone miner between the two halves of bronze, and left him there.

Then he stood in the bakery doorway and waited for the light. The first fishwife came round the corner with her cart, and stopped.
premise: Pell, the king's knife-bearer, wants to keep his sleepwalking king from walking into the shaft he ordered dug, but the only cure is to make someone hear what the king says asleep, and the court will not.

title: The Noon Star
content:
After the morning the city found its king kneeling in his nightshirt, the stone miner in the square began to speak. It spoke only after dark, and so softly that the sighted, with their lanterns and their looking, missed it. Ister heard it the first night. She had been blind since the summer before the collapse. She had put her best lens to the sun at noon, hunting a star her tables swore was there, and the sun went into her eyes and stayed.

The king came to her on the second evening, barefoot still. The council had let him keep his title and nothing that went with it, and he had nothing to do with his nights. "I know the way in the dark," he said, which was true, since he had walked it seventy times asleep. He put her hand on his forearm and led her down without a lamp, counting the steps aloud. She had once counted stars for him like that on the observatory roof. He had been the young hero who opened the red mountain, and she had been the woman who told him which days were lucky for digging.

The stone answered only confession. The king gave it one each night, kneeling between the halves of the plaque, and he had become fluent. In return the stone gave a piece of what the miner had seen from the bottom of the eighth shaft before the mountain closed. It was the sky, very small, as if seen through a straw, and in it, at noon, a single star. After the king's account of the props, the stone gave its declination. After his account of the overseer's warning, it gave the hour. Ister chalked each figure onto her slate by feel and lay awake reciting them.

On the last night of the month the stone said nothing to the king. Ister waited while the fountain dripped. At last the stone spoke one word to her, as if she had been standing there the whole time unaccounted for: "You."

She knew what it wanted. The almanac for that spring had shown a hard conjunction over the red mountain on the day of the deep dig. She had written *fair* beside it, because the king had promised her a lens from Venice, and she had wanted the lens more than she believed in conjunctions. The king's arm under her hand was warm. He was the only one in the city who still came for her. She could keep the six figures she had, guess the seventh, and come close.

"I gave you a good day," she said to the stone, loud enough for him to hear. "I saw the bad one and gave you a good day for a lens."

The stone told her the right ascension plainly, the way a man gives directions. The arm went out from under her hand. She heard his bare feet on the cobbles, heading not toward the palace but east, toward the dyer's quarter, where a vat was still steaming at that hour. She stood alone in a square she could not see and pressed the last number into the chalk dust on her own palm, so she would not lose it before she found the wall.
premise: Ister, a blind astronomer, wants the position of the one star she never saw, but the stone that knows it answers only confessions, and the last one it asks for would cost her the only friend who still walks her home.
